scenes.title: Deadlocks
scenes.narration: A deadlock happens when two transactions each hold a lock the other one needs, so both wait forever in a cycle unless the database intervenes.

scenes.title: How a deadlock forms
steps: Transaction A locks row 1, transaction B locks row 2
A now requests a lock on row 2, which B holds, so A waits
B now requests a lock on row 1, which A holds, so B waits
Neither can proceed: a circular wait, or deadlock
scenes.narration: Picture two transactions grabbing locks in opposite orders. A locks row one while B locks row two. Then A asks for row two, which B is holding, so A must wait. Meanwhile B asks for row one, which A is holding, so B must wait too. Each is waiting on the other, forming a circular dependency that can never resolve on its own.

scenes.title: A two-transaction deadlock
scenes.code:
-- Transaction A            -- Transaction B
BEGIN;                      BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts             UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 50  SET balance = balance - 50
WHERE id = 1;               WHERE id = 2;

-- A now wants row 2        -- B now wants row 1
UPDATE accounts             UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 50  SET balance = balance + 50
WHERE id = 2;  -- blocks     WHERE id = 1;  -- deadlock!
scenes.narration: Here are the two transactions side by side. A updates row one and B updates row two, so each holds an exclusive lock on a different row. Then A tries to update row two and blocks because B holds it. When B tries to update row one, it blocks on A, closing the cycle. The database detects this and cannot let both hang forever.

scenes.title: How the database resolves it
steps: The engine's deadlock detector spots the cycle in the wait graph
It picks a victim, often the transaction that is cheapest to undo
The victim is rolled back and its locks are released
The surviving transaction proceeds; the victim can be retried
scenes.narration: Databases run a deadlock detector that periodically checks the graph of who is waiting on whom. When it finds a cycle, it chooses a victim transaction, usually the one that is least expensive to abort. That victim is rolled back and its locks are freed, which lets the other transaction complete. Your application typically catches the deadlock error and simply retries the losing transaction.

scenes.title: Preventing deadlocks
bullets: Acquire locks in a consistent order across all transactions
Keep transactions short so locks are held briefly
Lower the isolation level where it is safe to reduce locking
Add retry logic so a victim transaction can run again
scenes.narration: You can make deadlocks rare with a few habits. The most powerful is acquiring locks in a consistent order everywhere, which makes circular waits impossible. Keeping transactions short shrinks the window for conflict. Using a lower isolation level where safe reduces the locks taken at all. And since deadlocks can never be fully eliminated, wrap transactions in retry logic so a rolled-back victim simply tries again.

scenes.text: Deadlocks are usually an ordering problem. If every transaction touches rows in the same order, the circular wait that causes them can never form.
scenes.narration: The core insight is that deadlocks are usually an ordering problem, and if every transaction touches rows in the same order, the circular wait simply cannot form.
